analysis.one_liner: Bans lead in toys and products for young children, with a small allowance for electronics.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban lead in children's products never got a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after being referred there the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to sell any product made for children under six that contains more lead than a set limit, with the limit tightening from 600 parts per million to 100 parts per million over two years [S2][S3]. The Consumer Product Safety Commission could tighten the limit further based on science, and electronics that cannot meet the limit would need child-resistant casings to keep lead away from children [S2][S3]. States would remain free to set stricter lead rules of their own [S3]. Lead exposure in young children can cause lasting developmental harm.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children under six, who would face less lead exposure from toys, and low-income families in particular, whose children are disproportionately exposed to lead. States that had passed their own stricter lead-in-toy laws would keep them without federal override [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It makes any children's product over the lead limit a banned hazardous substance under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, so selling it becomes unlawful rather than merely subject to recalls after the fact [S2][S3].
The limit tightens on a schedule — 600 parts per million immediately, 250 after one year, 100 after two — so manufacturers get notice while children get progressively better protection [S3].

It requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to revisit the standard five years after enactment and lower it to the lowest level that is feasible, so the ceiling ratchets down as technology improves [S2][S3].
It preserves stronger state and local lead laws, so no state's protections are weakened [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and sellers of toys and other products marketed for children under six, who would need to reformulate products with lead-free materials, test for lead, and pull noncompliant items from shelves. Electronics makers that cannot meet the limit would pay for child-resistant casings [S2][S3]. Some of these costs would likely show up in retail prices.

drawbacks.text: The cost falls on manufacturers and importers of children's products, especially small makers and importers who would face testing and reformulation expenses on tight margins [S2][S3].

A 100 parts per million limit within two years is strict by the standards of the time, and some electronic children's products could not meet it at all, which is why the bill allows child-resistant casings as a fallback instead of a true lead ban for those items [S2][S3].
The bill directs the Commission to lower the standard to the lowest 'feasible' level after five years, leaving a regulator significant discretion over how far costs could eventually climb [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the prevention of lead exposure to children under six during the years when lead does the most developmental damage, against compliance costs for toy makers and importers, some of which would be passed to consumers. The escalating limits give the industry time to adjust, and the electronics exception keeps the ban workable. On balance the protections are substantial and the costs are the ordinary price of removing a known poison from children's products.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee on the same day, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on October 3, 2007, with three Democratic cosponsors, during a period when lead-contaminated toys were being recalled [S1][S3][S4][S5].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection [S5].
The complete action history shows nothing after those referrals — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].

Congress did enact similar and stricter lead limits for children's products the following year in the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act of 2008, so the core idea eventually became law in that separate bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Children's product manufacturers and importers avoided the immediate compliance costs of a statutory lead ban, since this bill died without action; however, Congress passed comparable lead limits in a broader consumer product safety law the following year, so the industry's reprieve was temporary. Parents gained the protections through that later law rather than this one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Toy makers, only briefly; the idea became law in 2008

for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban lead in children's products.

for.name: Reps. Christopher Carney, Keith Ellison, and Bobby Rush

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by a Democrat in the 110th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die there.

sides.party_line_note: Only four Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no chamber ever voted on it, so the record shows no measurable partisan split — just a bill that never moved.

industries.note: The bill bans children's products above tightening lead limits, forcing toy makers and importers to use lead-free materials and test their products. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs against children's safety.

Electronics that cannot meet the lead limit would need child-resistant casings rather than a full ban, so these firms face compliance costs but get an accommodation unavailable to ordinary toy makers.
Retailers selling products for children under six would have to ensure the items they stock meet the lead limits, adding testing and sourcing burdens.
